title: Lifetimes in practice
description:
Write functions and a struct that return **borrowed** data from their inputs, with the lifetime annotations they need:

```rust
fn longest_word(text: &str) -> &str                          // the first longest word; "" for no words
fn pick<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str, first: bool) -> &'a str
fn split_pair(line: &str, sep: char) -> Option<(&str, &str)> // both parts trimmed; None without sep

struct Tokenizer<'a> { rest: &'a str }
impl<'a> Tokenizer<'a> {
    fn new(text: &'a str) -> Self
    fn next_token(&mut self) -> Option<&'a str>   // the next word, number or single punctuation character
}
```

`Tokenizer` skips white space; a token is a run of letters, a run of digits, or one other character. For `"x1 = 42+y;"` the tokens are `x`, `1`, `=`, `42`, `+`, `y`, `;`. The tokens borrow from the original text, so they stay valid after the tokenizer is gone.
hints: `longest_word` and `split_pair` have one input reference, so elision gives the output its lifetime: no annotations needed. `pick` has two, so it needs `'a`.

In `next_token`, `self.rest.trim_start()` drops the leading white space. `self.rest.find(|c: char| !c.is_alphabetic())` gives the byte position where a run of letters ends (`None` if it runs to the end; `c.is_ascii_digit()` tests for digits), and for one other character, `self.rest.char_indices().nth(1)` gives the byte position of the character after it (lesson 3.02). `split_at` then cuts the token off.

Return `Option<&'a str>` from `next_token`, not `Option<&str>`: the token borrows from the original text (lifetime `'a`), not from the tokenizer (`&mut self`), which is what lets the tokens outlive it.
